title: What is the relationship between parallelism and task slots in Flink (parallelism = number of subtasks per operator; each subtask needs a slot; parallelism must be ≤ total slots), and what does slot sharing (`SlotSharingGroup`) optimize?
shortTitle: What is the relationship between parallelism and task slots in Flink
keyPoints: Parallelism is the number of parallel subtasks an operator is split into, and each subtask needs exactly one task slot to execute.
A task slot is a unit of execution resource on a TaskManager representing a reserved share of its managed memory.
The maximum parallelism a job can run is capped by the total number of slots across all TaskManagers in the cluster.
Slot sharing lets subtasks from different operators share one slot, so a pipeline needs only as many slots as its highest operator parallelism.
Default slot sharing groups all operators together, which improves resource utilization and load balance by mixing heavy and light operators.
You can isolate resource-hungry operators into separate slot sharing groups so they get dedicated slots.
Operator chaining fuses consecutive forwarding operators into a single task thread within a slot, eliminating serialization overhead.

s1_definition.oneliner: Parallelism is subtasks per operator and each subtask needs a slot, so parallelism is capped by total slots, and slot sharing lets different operators' subtasks share one slot so a pipeline needs only as many slots as its highest parallelism.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Parallelism** – The number of parallel subtasks an operator is split into, where each subtask processes a slice of the data stream independently.
- **Task slot** – A unit of execution resource on a TaskManager that represents a reserved share of its managed memory and can host one or more subtasks.
- **Slot constraint** – The job's maximum parallelism cannot exceed the total number of slots available across all TaskManagers.
- **Slot sharing** – A mechanism that lets subtasks from different operators of the same job run together in one slot, reducing the total slots needed to the highest operator parallelism.
- **Slot sharing group** – A named group that controls which operators may share slots, letting you isolate resource-hungry operators into dedicated slots.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India processing fraud checks on a conveyor line with several stations: receive the transaction, look up the account, score the fraud risk, and raise an alert. Parallelism is how many copies of the conveyor line you run side by side, say four lines to handle four transactions at once. A task slot is a desk where a worker can sit. Slot sharing is the clever arrangement where one worker at a single desk handles all four stations for one transaction in sequence, so you only need four desks, one per line, instead of sixteen. Fewer desks, same throughput.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In Flink, parallelism is the number of parallel subtasks an operator is split into, and a task slot is the runtime's unit of execution resource on a TaskManager, representing a reserved share of its managed memory. Every parallel subtask needs a slot to run, so the fundamental relationship is that the parallelism you can actually run is capped by the total number of slots in the cluster, which is the slots-per-TaskManager setting times the number of TaskManagers.

Slot sharing addresses the efficiency problem. Without it, a pipeline of four operators each at parallelism four would need sixteen slots. With default slot sharing, one subtask from each operator shares a single slot, so a slot runs the source, keyBy, scoring, and sink subtasks of the same parallel pipeline instance. The result is that the slots a job needs equal the maximum parallelism among its operators, not the sum. This also improves load balance because mixing one of each operator per slot spreads an expensive operator's work evenly instead of concentrating it.

At the National Bank of India our fraud pipeline had four operators at parallelism four, and the team initially provisioned sixteen slots assuming each subtask needed its own slot. Once we understood default slot sharing, we saw it needed only four slots, each running a complete source-to-sink slice, which let us run the same throughput on a much smaller cluster. When the ML scoring step became extremely CPU-heavy, we isolated it into its own slot sharing group for dedicated slots, understanding that this raised the total slot requirement from four to eight.

The rules I apply are to size parallelism to throughput and key cardinality, ensure total slots at least equal the maximum parallelism, rely on default slot sharing for efficiency, and isolate only the operators that genuinely need dedicated resources.

Remember one sentence: Slot sharing lets a full pipeline share one slot per parallel instance so you need only max-parallelism slots, not sum-of-all-operator subtasks.
